Newly hatched golden eagle chicks are surprisingly small given the substantial adult size of this apex predator, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 105 grams [Wwb = approximately 105 grams]. This modest neonatal mass contrasts sharply with the dramatic growth that occurs over the subsequent weeks. The incubation period for eggs is relatively prolonged, with hatching occurring after 44 days [ab = 44 days] when maintained at a developmental temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This incubation duration, derived from comparative data on large raptors including the osprey and bald eagle, reflects the substantial energetic investment required to produce a viable, well-developed hatchling. Upon emergence, the altricial nestling is entirely dependent on its parents for both warmth and food provisioning, setting the stage for an intense period of somatic growth. The downy chick is brooded nearly continuously during its first week, a critical phase during which thermoregulatory capacity begins to develop. Field studies indicate that this initial mass serves as a baseline from which the rapid, sigmoidal growth trajectory characteristic of large accipitrids proceeds, ultimately leading to the species' impressive adult body dimensions.

The ultimate wet weight for females reaches an average of 5194 grams [Wwi = 5194 grams], whereas males attain a considerably smaller ultimate wet weight of 3572 grams [Wwi = 3572 grams], representing one of the more pronounced examples of reverse sexual size dimorphism among diurnal raptors. This size disparity, in which females are roughly 45% heavier than males, is thought to facilitate partitioning of prey resources and to allow the larger female to better defend the nest and incubate eggs effectively. The growth rate of nestlings is correspondingly rapid; under typical thermal conditions maintained by the attending parents (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the time since birth at fledging is approximately 67.5 days [tx = approximately 67.5 days]. This milestone marks the point at which the juvenile bird achieves its first sustained flight, although parental provisioning often continues for several more weeks as the young eagle hones its hunting skills. The energetic demands of this rapid growth are considerable, requiring the adults to deliver a substantial biomass of prey, predominantly lagomorphs and ground squirrels, to the developing nestlings throughout the nestling period.

Under controlled thermal conditions typical of active metabolic regulation by the brooding adult, quantified at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 202.5 days [tp = approximately 202.5 days]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity for a large raptor is notable, although it must be emphasized that while gonadal development may be complete, actual breeding is typically deferred for several additional years. The reproductive strategy of the golden eagle is characterized by low fecundity but high parental investment. Females typically lay between 1 and 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 3 eggs per clutch], and they ordinarily produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This modest annual reproductive output is compensated by extensive biparental care, including prolonged post-fledging dependence, which significantly enhances juvenile survival. The maximum reproductive rate observed in this species reflects a life-history strategy evolved for stability and longevity in a harsh, resource-limited environment, where each breeding attempt represents a substantial commitment of time and energy.

The age at which these formidable raptors commence their first successful breeding attempt is a critical life-history parameter. Field observations of marked populations indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 1460 days [tR = 1460 days], corresponding to approximately four years of age. at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]The extended interval between fledging and first reproduction is a common feature among large, long-lived birds of prey, allowing the young eagle to acquire the complex hunting skills and establish a high-quality territory necessary for successful nesting. Throughout this prolonged juvenile and sub-adult period, the bird undergoes a gradual plumage maturation sequence, transitioning from the dark juvenile feathers with extensive white patches to the classic dark brown adult plumage with golden hackles on the nape. This deferred maturity, viewed through the lens of life-history theory, represents a trade-off between immediate reproductive potential and investment in future survival and reproductive success. The delay also allows for the full development of the skeletal and muscular systems required to take and defend large prey, a crucial adaptation given the species' role as an apex predator in its ecosystem.

One of the most remarkable features of golden eagle life history is its extreme longevity. The maximum lifespan documented for this species reaches 17520 days [am = 17520 days], a total of 48 years, when measured at an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This exceptional lifespan, among the longest recorded for any bird of prey, underscores a life-history strategy heavily weighted toward adult survival rather than high fecundity. Such longevity allows for multiple reproductive attempts across a long breeding career, partially offsetting the species' low annual productivity. Wild populations in stable environments with abundant prey can exhibit remarkably high annual adult survival rates, often exceeding 90%, which is a key demographic parameter sustaining population viability. The combination of delayed maturity, low fecundity, and exceptional longevity places the golden eagle firmly at the slow end of the life-history continuum, a strategy well-suited to its position as a long-lived, K-selected apex predator occupying stable, resource-predictable territories across its expansive Holarctic range.
